rewritten_text:
“I hope I shall soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” Mr. Weston said.

Mrs. Elton was quite ready to take this hope as a special compliment to herself and smiled warmly.

“I expect you have heard of a certain Frank Churchill,” he continued, “and know that he is my son, although his surname is different.”

“Oh, yes, and I shall be very happy to meet him. I am sure Mr. Elton will visit him as soon as possible, and we shall both be delighted to welcome him to the Vicarage.”

“You are very kind. Frank will be delighted too, I’m sure. He is coming to London next week, perhaps sooner. We heard in a letter today. I came across the letters on my way this morning, and when I recognized my son’s handwriting, I took the liberty of opening his—although it was addressed to Mrs. Weston. She is the one he usually writes to, I assure you. I hardly ever receive a letter.”

“So you actually opened a letter addressed to her! Oh, Mr. Weston”—she gave an affected laugh—“I must object to that. What a dangerous example to set! Please don’t let your neighbors copy you. Really, if this is what I have to expect, we married women must start standing up for ourselves! Oh, Mr. Weston, I would never have thought it of you!”

“Yes, we men are terrible fellows. You must look after yourself, Mrs. Elton. This letter tells us—it is a short letter, written in a hurry simply to let us know—that they are all coming to London immediately because of Mrs. Churchill. She has been unwell all winter and thinks Enscombe is too cold for her, so they are all moving south without delay.”

“Really! From Yorkshire, I believe. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, about a hundred and ninety miles from London. A considerable journey.”

“Yes, indeed, a very considerable one. Sixty-five miles farther than Maple Grove is from London. But what does distance matter to wealthy people, Mr. Weston? You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, rushes about sometimes. You will hardly believe this, but twice in a single week he and Mr. Bragge traveled to London and back with four horses.”

“The difficulty with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand it, has been unable to get off the sofa for a whole week at a time. In Frank’s last letter, he said she complained of being too weak to reach her conservatory without leaning on both his arm and his uncle’s!”

Tom managed to score the cupboard with it and was preparing an attack on the bureau when he was summoned away to dress for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a cake of soap. He carried them outside and placed the basin on a small bench by the door; then he dipped the soap into the water and set it down, rolled up his sleeves, gently emptied the water onto the ground, and returned to the kitchen, where he began industriously drying his face on the towel behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said:

“Now, ain’t you ashamed of yourself, Tom? You mustn’t behave so badly. Water won’t do you any harm.”

Tom was somewhat put out. They filled the basin again, and this time he lingered over it, summoning his courage, drew a great breath, and set to work. Presently he came into the kitchen with his eyes squeezed shut, feeling about for the towel, while an honorable evidence of soap and water dripped from his face. Yet when he came out of the towel he still failed to satisfy, for his clean region ended at his chin and jaws, like a mask; beyond that boundary stretched a dark tract of unwatered earth, running down the front and backward about his neck. Mary undertook the work herself, and by the time she finished he was a man and a brother, with no distinction of color. His drenched hair was brushed tidily, its little curls arranged in a delicate, symmetrical whole. [In private he laboriously flattened the curls and plastered the hair against his head; he considered curls unmanly, and his own were a constant source of bitterness.] Mary then brought out a suit he had worn solely on Sundays for two years. They were known simply as his “other clothes,” which tells us the extent of his wardrobe. After he dressed, the girl “set him to rights”: she buttoned his tidy roundabout to his chin, folded his immense shirt collar down across his shoulders, brushed him, and topped him with his speckled straw hat. His appearance was now vastly improved and profoundly uncomfortable. He felt every bit as uncomfortable as he appeared, for the restrictions of untorn clothes and cleanliness chafed him. He trusted that Mary might overlook his shoes, but this hope came to nothing. She covered them generously with tallow, according to custom, and produced them. Losing his temper, he declared that he was always being forced to do everything he did not wish to do.

The following day he stayed indoors, spending most of it in his room, sick with an overwhelming fear of death and yet indifferent to living. The sense that he was being hunted, trapped, and pursued had begun to take possession of him. A mere flutter of the tapestry in the wind made him tremble. Dead leaves striking the leaded windows seemed like his own squandered resolutions and desperate regrets. Whenever he shut his eyes, he saw the sailor’s face again, peering through the misted glass, and felt horror once more grip his heart.

Perhaps, though, his imagination alone had summoned vengeance from the darkness and placed those dreadful forms of punishment before him. Real life was chaotic, but imagination had a terrifying logic. Imagination made remorse follow at the heels of sin. Imagination gave every crime its deformed offspring. In the ordinary world of facts, the wicked went unpunished and the good unrewarded. The strong received success; failure was forced upon the weak. That was all. Besides, if a stranger had been prowling around the house, the servants or gamekeepers would have noticed him. If there had been footprints in the flower beds, the gardeners would have reported them. Yes, it had only been imagination. Sibyl Vane’s brother had not returned to murder him. He had sailed off in his ship to sink in some winter sea. From that man, at least, he was safe. After all, the man did not know who he was, could not possibly know. His youthful appearance had been a mask that saved him.

Yet if it had only been an illusion, how dreadful to think that conscience could summon such terrifying apparitions, give them a visible shape, and make them move before his eyes! What would his life become if, night and day, shadows of his crime peered out at him from quiet corners, mocked him from hidden places, whispered into his ear while he sat at a feast, and woke him with freezing fingers while he slept? As the thought moved through his mind, his face grew white with terror, and the air seemed suddenly colder. Oh, what a frenzied hour of madness had driven him to kill his friend! How appalling even the memory of that scene was! He saw the whole thing again. Every hideous detail returned with fresh horror. From the black cavern of time, terrible and wrapped in scarlet, the image of his sin arose.
